title: Argus: A Cross-Regime Study of Uncertainty Quantification Transferability in Single-Step GUI Grounding
claim: Method rankings transfer strongly within a fixed model or vendor but weaken across models and interfaces, and can even invert.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmap panels, diagonal blocks outlined, shared diverging colorbars
description: Two square correlation heatmaps sit side by side. Each cell holds a Spearman rho value. The left panel is 16x16 and covers four open-weight models (Q7, Q72, UI, PT) crossed with four datasets (V2, SP, OSG, UIV). It is mostly warm red with high values, and the darkest cells fall inside the black-outlined diagonal blocks. The right panel is 12x12 and covers closed-source vendors (GPT, Sonnet, Gemini) crossed with the same datasets. It is far more mixed: strong blue negative correlations (down to about -0.8) appear off the diagonal, while the Gemini block is dark red. Each panel has a diverging red-white-blue colorbar from -1 to 1 and rotated axis labels. The eye goes first to the dark diagonal blocks and the blue patches on the right.
caption: Full-method ranking transfer. Spearman ρ between per-cell rankings (50-seed means). Left: 27-method open-weight, 16 cells. Right: 8-method API-only, 12 cells. Diagonal blocks: within-model or within-vendor transfer.
abstract: Single-step GUI grounding for computer-use agents turns visual predictions into executable clicks, so uncertainty estimates must support rejection, calibration, miss-severity ranking, and spatial safety regions. Existing post-hoc uncertainty quantification (UQ) evidence is fragmented across isolated model and dataset pairs, leaving unclear whether UQ rankings remain stable when the agent, benchmark, or observable interface changes. We present a cross-regime study of post-hoc UQ in single-step executable GUI grounding, covering a 27-method, seven-family open-weight matrix over 4 GUI-grounding VLM agents and 4 datasets, plus an 8-method API-compatible closed-source matrix across 3 frontier vendors where logits, hidden states, and attention maps are unavailable. The main finding is selective transfer: for error detection and selective execution, UQ rankings are stable across datasets for a fixed model, but degrade across model classes and observable interfaces. Hidden-state and density methods form the most stable open-weight family, while CoCoA-1MCA, Focus, sampling-based scores, and verbalised self-assessment win in specific regimes. Ranking transfer is strongest within a fixed model across datasets, reaching Spearman $\rho=0.969$ and averaging $\rho=0.794$ over 24 same-model pairs, with mean $\rho=0.705$ over all 120 open-weight pairs. In contrast, cross-tier transfer to closed-source vendors is much weaker: Spearman $\rho$ averages only $+0.08$ over 12 vendor x dataset pairs on the shared 8-method intersection, so closed-source UQ recommendations should be reranked on the target rather than extrapolated. Model-class transitions further reshape UQ preferences: attention, verbalised, and VLM-native families lose AUROC on every dataset, while density methods remain stable, and a scale-only baseline shows that logit-family degradation on ScreenSpot-Pro is partly confounded by scale rather than grounding fine-tuning alone. Finally, conformal click regions show that score-level discrimination is not enough for deployment: locally weighted disks can shrink radii by up to $38\%$ when the plug-in UQ suits the regime, but they can also enlarge radii, and coverage can degrade under calibration-test or interface mismatch. We release per-item records, calibration/test splits, UQ scores, and analysis scripts as a reproducible basis for regime-aware UQ selection in GUI agents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/divake/argus-uq.
